about: Mechatronics 1 (MECH40004) is a core Year 1 module on Imperial's MEng Mechanical Engineering, running across the year. It teaches students to model electrical circuits in a way that is compatible with mechanical systems, and to select components for simple electromechanical systems, using ideas with direct mechanical equivalents such as equivalent characteristics, operating diagrams and complex impedance. The topics follow the list recorded from the department's module descriptor (which could not be re-read when this pack was written), supported by a third-party course summary last reviewed in 2021-22. Assessment details could not be confirmed, so check the department's module page.

notes.h: Circuit elements and their mechanical equivalents
notes.body:
Mechatronics treats electrical and mechanical parts of a machine as one system, so circuit elements are described in a way that maps directly onto springs, masses and dampers.

Variables
- Current i (A): rate of flow of charge, i = dq/dt.
- Voltage v (V): energy per unit charge between two points (potential difference).
- Power p = vi (W). Use the passive sign convention: if current enters the + terminal, p > 0 means the element absorbs power.

Ideal sources
- Ideal voltage source: fixed voltage whatever the current. Ideal current source: fixed current whatever the voltage.
- Real sources are modelled as an ideal source with an internal resistance (in series for a voltage source).

Resistor
- Ohm's law: v = iR. Power dissipated: p = i²R = v²/R.
- Series: R = R₁ + R₂ + ...; parallel: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + ...; two in parallel: R₁R₂/(R₁ + R₂).
- Example: 10 Ω in parallel with 15 Ω is 6 Ω; adding 4 Ω in series gives 10 Ω. From 12 V this draws 1.2 A, and the 4 Ω resistor drops 4.8 V.
- Voltage divider: v_out = v_in R₂/(R₁ + R₂) (unloaded). Current divider: the current splits in inverse proportion to resistance.

Capacitor
- i = C dv/dt; charge q = Cv; energy stored ½Cv².
- The voltage across a capacitor cannot change instantaneously (it would need infinite current).
- Under steady DC it carries no current: it behaves as an open circuit.
- Parallel capacitors add; series capacitors combine like parallel resistors.

Inductor
- v = L di/dt; energy stored ½Li².
- The current through an inductor cannot change instantaneously; interrupting it suddenly creates a large voltage spike (hence flyback diodes across relay coils and motors).
- Under steady DC it behaves as a short circuit (apart from its winding resistance).
- Series inductors add.

Mechanical analogies
Writing the element laws side by side shows the parallel with mechanical elements.
Force–voltage analogy (force ↔ voltage, velocity ↔ current):
- mass m (F = m dv/dt) ↔ inductor L (v = L di/dt);
- damper c (F = cv) ↔ resistor R;
- spring k (F = k∫v dt) ↔ capacitor with 1/C = k.
Force–current analogy (force ↔ current, velocity ↔ voltage):
- mass ↔ capacitor; damper ↔ conductance 1/R; spring ↔ 1/L.
In both, springs and masses (like capacitors and inductors) store energy, while dampers (like resistors) dissipate it. This lets one set of tools (equivalent circuits, impedance, transient response) describe a complete electromechanical system.

Exam tips: state which analogy you are using, check the energy-storage elements against their continuity rules (capacitor voltage, inductor current), and always include units.

Engineers describe time-varying voltages and currents (and the sensor signals that represent mechanical quantities) using a small set of measures.

Periodic waveforms
- Period T (s) and frequency f = 1/T (Hz); angular frequency ω = 2πf (rad/s).
- Sine wave: v(t) = V_p sin(ωt + φ), with peak V_p, peak-to-peak 2V_p and phase φ.
- Other common shapes: square, triangular, sawtooth, pulse trains.

Mean and RMS values
- Mean (average): V_mean = (1/T)∫v dt over one period. A pure sine has zero mean; a half-wave rectified sine has mean V_p/π; a full-wave rectified sine 2V_p/π.
- Root mean square: V_rms = √[(1/T)∫v² dt]. The RMS value is the DC voltage that would deliver the same average power to a resistor.
- Sine: V_rms = V_p/√2 ≈ 0.707V_p. UK mains is 230 V rms at 50 Hz, so the peak is about 325 V.
- Square wave of ±V: V_rms = V.

Pulse-width modulation (PWM)
A fixed-frequency square wave switching between 0 and V with duty cycle D (fraction of the period spent on). The mean is DV and the RMS is V√D. PWM is used to control motor speed and LED brightness efficiently: a 12 V supply at 25% duty gives a 3 V mean (RMS 6 V). The switching frequency is chosen high enough that the motor's inductance and inertia smooth the current and speed.

Decibels
Gain in dB = 20 log₁₀(V₂/V₁) for voltage ratios (10 log₁₀ for power ratios). Halving a voltage is about −6 dB; a factor of 1/√2 is about −3 dB; a factor of 10 is +20 dB.

Analogue and digital signals
- An analogue signal varies continuously; a digital signal takes discrete levels (usually two: logic 0 and 1).
- An analogue-to-digital converter (ADC) samples the signal at regular intervals and quantises each sample. An n-bit ADC with reference V_ref has 2ⁿ levels and resolution V_ref/2ⁿ: a 10-bit, 5 V ADC resolves about 4.9 mV; a 12-bit one about 1.2 mV.

Sampling and aliasing
- The Nyquist criterion: sample at more than twice the highest frequency present (f_s > 2f_max) to represent the signal without ambiguity.
- If a component above f_s/2 is present, it appears as a false lower frequency (aliasing). An analogue low-pass (anti-aliasing) filter before the ADC prevents this.

Noise and signal conditioning
Sensor signals are often small and noisy. Amplification, filtering (low-pass, high-pass, band-pass) and shielding are used before conversion. A signal-to-noise ratio is often quoted in dB.

Exam tips: be precise about whether a value is peak, peak-to-peak, mean or RMS, and convert before using P = V²/R (which needs RMS values for AC power).

Digital systems represent information with two levels, 0 and 1 (for example 0 V and 5 V or 3.3 V). Logic is used in mechatronics for interlocks, sequencing and the interface to microcontrollers.

Number systems
- Binary (base 2): 1011₂ = 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11.
- Hexadecimal (base 16, digits 0–9 and A–F): each hex digit is four bits, e.g. 1011 0110₂ = B6₁₆ = 182.
- An n-bit unsigned number ranges from 0 to 2ⁿ − 1 (0–255 for 8 bits).

Basic gates
- NOT: output is the inverse of the input (Ā).
- AND: 1 only if all inputs are 1 (A·B).
- OR: 1 if any input is 1 (A + B).
- NAND and NOR: AND and OR followed by NOT.
- XOR: 1 if the inputs differ (A ⊕ B = ĀB + AB̄).
NAND alone (or NOR alone) can make every other function, so each is called a universal gate.

Boolean algebra
- A + 0 = A, A·1 = A, A + 1 = 1, A·0 = 0.
- A + A = A, A·A = A, A + Ā = 1, A·Ā = 0.
- Distributive: A(B + C) = AB + AC; also A + BC = (A + B)(A + C).
- Absorption: A + AB = A; A(A + B) = A.
- De Morgan's theorems: (A·B)̄ = Ā + B̄ and (A + B)̄ = Ā·B̄. "Break the bar, change the sign."
Example: AB + AB̄ = A(B + B̄) = A.

From a specification to a circuit
1. Write a truth table listing every input combination (2ⁿ rows for n inputs).
2. Write a sum-of-products expression: one AND term for each row where the output is 1, OR-ed together.
3. Simplify with Boolean algebra or a Karnaugh map, which groups adjacent 1s (in groups of 1, 2, 4, 8) so that each group removes a variable.
4. Draw the gate circuit and, if wanted, convert to NAND-only using De Morgan.

Worked example: a press guard
A press may operate (Y = 1) only if both hand buttons are pressed (A = B = 1) and the guard is closed (G = 1), or if a maintenance key K is turned and the guard is closed. Y = G(AB + K). This needs one two-input AND for AB, an OR with K, and a final AND with G.

Combinational and sequential logic
- Combinational logic: outputs depend only on present inputs (gates, decoders, multiplexers).
- Sequential logic: outputs also depend on past inputs, using memory elements such as latches and flip-flops; counters and registers are built from them. A microcontroller carries out logic in software, but the same Boolean reasoning applies.

Practical points (background)
Mechanical switches bounce, giving several rapid transitions; they are debounced in hardware (RC filter and Schmitt trigger) or in software. Inputs should never float: use pull-up or pull-down resistors.

Exam tips: always present a full truth table, and check a simplified expression against it row by row.

A transducer converts energy from one form to another; a sensor is a transducer that produces a signal related to a measured quantity (displacement, force, temperature, speed). Actuators do the reverse, turning electrical signals into motion.

Sensor characteristics
- Range and span: the limits of the input that can be measured.
- Sensitivity: change in output per unit change in input (e.g. mV/°C).
- Resolution: smallest detectable change in input.
- Accuracy: closeness to the true value; precision (repeatability): closeness of repeated readings.
- Linearity: how closely the output follows a straight line.
- Hysteresis: different outputs for the same input depending on whether it is rising or falling.
- Dynamic response: how quickly the output follows a changing input (time constant, bandwidth).

Displacement and position
- Potentiometer: a wiper on a resistive track gives v_out proportional to position. Simple and cheap, but it wears; loading by the measuring circuit makes it non-linear.
- Linear variable differential transformer (LVDT): a movable core changes the coupling between a primary and two secondary coils; non-contact and very fine resolution.
- Optical incremental encoder: a slotted disc interrupts light to give pulses. With N lines per revolution the resolution is 360°/N; two channels in quadrature give direction and allow ×4 counting (500 lines → 0.72° per line, 0.18° with ×4 decoding).
- Absolute encoders give a unique code for every position.

Strain and force
- A bonded metal-foil strain gauge changes resistance with strain: gauge factor GF = (ΔR/R)/ε, typically about 2 for metal foil (approximate).
- Example: a 120 Ω gauge with GF = 2.0 at 500 με changes by ΔR = 2 × 500 × 10⁻⁶ × 120 = 0.12 Ω, far too small to read directly.
- A Wheatstone bridge converts small resistance changes into a voltage. For a quarter bridge (one active gauge) with supply V_s, v_out ≈ V_s GF ε/4. With V_s = 5 V the example gives about 1.25 mV, which is then amplified.
- Half and full bridges use two or four active gauges, increasing sensitivity and cancelling temperature effects.
- Load cells are elastic elements fitted with gauges to measure force.

Temperature
- Thermocouple: two dissimilar metals produce a small voltage that depends on the temperature difference between the hot and reference junctions (Seebeck effect); type K gives roughly 41 μV/°C (approximate). Wide range, rugged, needs cold-junction compensation.
- Resistance temperature detector (RTD), e.g. Pt100: 100 Ω at 0 °C, rising by about 0.385 Ω/°C (approximate), so about 138.5 Ω at 100 °C. Accurate and stable.
- Thermistor: semiconductor with large, non-linear resistance change (usually negative temperature coefficient); very sensitive over a narrow range.

Speed and other sensors
Tachogenerators (voltage proportional to speed), encoders (pulse frequency), Hall-effect sensors (magnetic field, used for position and current), accelerometers (often MEMS), and proximity switches.

Signal conditioning
Most sensor outputs need amplification (often an operational amplifier), filtering, and conversion (ADC) before a controller can use them.

Exam tips: give a numerical sensitivity where you can, and for bridges explain why the bridge is used (to measure a small change on top of a large base value).

notes.h: DC networks, equivalent circuits and transients
notes.body:
Kirchhoff's laws
- Kirchhoff's current law (KCL): the currents entering a node sum to zero (conservation of charge).
- Kirchhoff's voltage law (KVL): the voltages around any closed loop sum to zero (conservation of energy).
Nodal analysis applies KCL at each unknown node voltage; mesh analysis applies KVL around loops. Superposition: in a linear circuit, the response to several sources is the sum of the responses to each acting alone (other voltage sources shorted, current sources opened).

Thévenin and Norton equivalents ("equivalent characteristics")
Any linear two-terminal network can be replaced, as seen from its terminals, by:
- Thévenin: a voltage source V_Th in series with R_Th;
- Norton: a current source I_N = V_Th/R_Th in parallel with R_Th.
V_Th is the open-circuit voltage; I_N is the short-circuit current; R_Th is the resistance seen with sources turned off (or V_oc/I_sc). The network's terminal characteristic is a straight line on a v–i graph from (0, V_Th) to (I_N, 0).

Example: 12 V supplying a divider of R₁ = 6 kΩ (top) and R₂ = 3 kΩ (bottom), output across R₂.
- V_Th = 12 × 3/9 = 4 V; R_Th = 6 ∥ 3 = 2 kΩ.
- With a 2 kΩ load: v = 4 × 2/(2 + 2) = 2 V.

Operating points and load lines
Plot the source characteristic (a line from V_Th to I_N) and the load characteristic on the same axes; they intersect at the operating point. This graphical "operating diagram" works even for non-linear loads such as diodes, lamps or motors, and has a direct mechanical parallel (a motor's torque–speed line against a load's torque–speed curve).

Maximum power transfer
A load receives maximum power when R_L = R_Th; then P_max = V_Th²/(4R_Th) and the efficiency is only 50%. In the example, P_max = 16/(4 × 2000) = 2 mW.

First-order transients
When a switch operates, energy stored in a capacitor or inductor cannot change instantly, so the circuit responds exponentially with time constant τ:
- RC circuit: τ = RC. Charging from 0 towards V: v_C(t) = V(1 − e^(−t/τ)). Discharging: v_C = V₀e^(−t/τ).
- RL circuit: τ = L/R. Current rises as i(t) = (V/R)(1 − e^(−t/τ)).
- After τ the response has completed 63.2% of its change; after 5τ, more than 99%. Time to reach 90% is τ ln 10 ≈ 2.3τ.
General method: x(t) = x(∞) + [x(0⁺) − x(∞)]e^(−t/τ), where τ uses the Thévenin resistance seen by the C or L.

Example: R = 10 kΩ, C = 100 μF, so τ = 1 s. Charging from 12 V, after 2 s v_C = 12(1 − e⁻²) = 10.4 V.

Mechanical parallel
A mass with viscous damping driven by a constant force reaches its terminal speed exponentially with τ = m/c, exactly like current in an RL circuit (τ = L/R).

Exam tips: find initial and final values first (capacitor open, inductor short at DC steady state), then τ from the resistance seen by the energy-storage element.

A diode is a two-terminal semiconductor device (a pn junction) that conducts easily in one direction and blocks in the other. It is the simplest non-linear circuit element.

Characteristics
- Forward bias (anode positive): little current until about 0.6–0.7 V for silicon (approximate), then the current rises steeply.
- Reverse bias: only a tiny leakage current, until the reverse breakdown voltage is reached.
- Models: ideal diode (short circuit forward, open circuit reverse); constant-voltage-drop model (a 0.7 V drop when conducting); more detailed models add a series resistance.
- Diode problems are often solved by assuming a state (on or off), solving, then checking consistency.

Half-wave rectifier
A single diode in series with the load passes only the positive half-cycles. The output peak is V_p − 0.7 V; the mean of the ideal output is V_p/π. Only half the input cycle is used.

Full-wave bridge rectifier
Four diodes route both half-cycles through the load in the same direction. Two diodes conduct at a time, so the output peak is about V_p − 1.4 V. The ripple frequency is twice the supply frequency (100 Hz from 50 Hz mains). Each diode must withstand a peak reverse voltage of about V_p.

Smoothing
A reservoir capacitor C across the load charges to the peak and then supplies the load between peaks. For load current I and ripple frequency f_r, the peak-to-peak ripple is approximately ΔV ≈ I/(f_r C), where f_r = f for half-wave and 2f for full-wave.
Example: a 12 V rms transformer secondary has a peak of 12√2 = 16.97 V. After a bridge, the peak output is about 15.6 V. With a 0.5 A load and C = 2200 μF on 50 Hz mains (100 Hz ripple): ΔV ≈ 0.5/(100 × 2200 × 10⁻⁶) = 2.3 V. Halving the ripple needs double the capacitance.

Zener diodes and regulation
A Zener diode is designed to operate in reverse breakdown, holding a nearly constant voltage V_Z. With a series resistor it forms a simple voltage regulator: the resistor drops the excess voltage, and the Zener current changes to absorb changes in load or supply. Integrated linear regulators (e.g. fixed 5 V devices) are more commonly used today.

Other diode applications
- Light-emitting diodes (LEDs): forward voltage roughly 2 V for red, higher for blue/white (approximate). They need a series resistor: R = (V_s − V_f)/I. For 5 V, V_f = 2 V and 20 mA, R = 150 Ω.
- Flyback (freewheeling) diode: placed in reverse across a relay coil or motor. When the switch opens, the inductor current continues through the diode instead of producing a large voltage spike (v = L di/dt) that could destroy the switching transistor.
- Protection against reverse polarity, signal clamping, and logic gating.

Exam tips: draw the current path for each half-cycle of a bridge, remember there are two diode drops, and state the ripple frequency correctly when using ΔV ≈ I/(f_r C).

notes.h: AC networks: phasors and complex impedance
notes.body:
In a linear circuit driven by a sinusoid of angular frequency ω, every voltage and current in the steady state is a sinusoid at the same frequency, differing only in amplitude and phase. Phasors and complex impedance turn the differential equations into algebra.

Phasors
A sinusoid v(t) = V_p cos(ωt + φ) is represented by the complex number V = V e^(jφ) (using either peak or, more commonly in power work, RMS magnitude). Engineers write j = √(−1). Differentiation becomes multiplication by jω.

Complex impedance Z = V/I
- Resistor: Z_R = R (current in phase with voltage).
- Inductor: Z_L = jωL; reactance X_L = ωL; current lags voltage by 90°.
- Capacitor: Z_C = 1/(jωC) = −j/(ωC); reactance X_C = 1/(ωC); current leads voltage by 90°.
Impedances combine exactly like resistances: series add, parallel combine as reciprocals. So all the DC methods (KCL, KVL, Thévenin) carry over with complex numbers.

Worked example: series RL load on mains
R = 100 Ω and L = 0.5 H in series on 230 V rms, 50 Hz.
- ω = 2π × 50 = 314.2 rad/s; X_L = 157.1 Ω.
- Z = 100 + j157.1 Ω; |Z| = √(100² + 157.1²) = 186.2 Ω; phase angle φ = arctan(157.1/100) = 57.5°.
- I = 230/186.2 = 1.24 A rms, lagging the voltage by 57.5°.
- Real power P = I²R = 152.6 W; apparent power S = VI = 284 VA; power factor cos φ = 0.537 (lagging).

AC power
- Real (average) power P = V_rms I_rms cos φ (W): only resistance dissipates it.
- Reactive power Q = V_rms I_rms sin φ (var): energy that sloshes back and forth in L and C.
- Apparent power S = V_rms I_rms (VA), with S² = P² + Q².
- Power factor = cos φ. A low power factor needs more current for the same useful power; inductive loads (motors) are often corrected with parallel capacitors.

Frequency response and filters
Because reactances depend on ω, circuits behave differently at different frequencies.
- RC low-pass filter (output across C): gain 1/√(1 + (ωRC)²); cut-off (−3 dB) frequency f_c = 1/(2πRC). For R = 1 kΩ and C = 1 μF, f_c ≈ 159 Hz. Above f_c the gain falls by 20 dB per decade.
- Swapping R and C gives a high-pass filter with the same f_c.
- Series RLC resonance at ω₀ = 1/√(LC): X_L = X_C, the impedance is purely resistive and minimum.

Mechanical equivalents
A spring–mass–damper under sinusoidal forcing is analysed the same way: mechanical impedance F/v gives jωm for a mass, c for a damper and k/(jω) for a spring. Resonance occurs at ω₀ = √(k/m), the analogue of 1/√(LC).

Exam tips: work in RMS values for power, keep track of whether the angle is of Z, V or I, and draw a phasor diagram as a check on lagging versus leading.

notes.h: Electromagnetic actuators: DC motors and their operating diagrams
notes.body:
Electromagnetic actuators convert electrical energy into motion using magnetic forces. The DC motor is the main example in a first course, because its model links electrical and mechanical quantities neatly.

Force on a conductor
A conductor of length L carrying current I perpendicular to a magnetic field of flux density B feels a force F = BIL (Fleming's left-hand rule gives the direction). In a motor these forces on the armature windings produce a torque.

Permanent-magnet DC motor model
With field flux fixed, the motor is described by one constant k (the torque constant in N m/A equals the back-emf constant in V s/rad, in SI units):
- Torque: T = kI.
- Back emf: E = kω (the rotating armature acts as a generator opposing the supply).
- Armature circuit (steady state): V = IR + kω, where R is the armature resistance.
Combining: ω = V/k − (R/k²)T. The torque–speed characteristic is a straight line.

Key points of the line
- No-load speed (T = 0): ω₀ = V/k.
- Stall torque (ω = 0): T_s = kV/R, with stall current V/R.
- Mechanical output power P = Tω is a parabola, maximum at half stall torque and half no-load speed: P_max = V²/(4R) (the electrical analogue is maximum power transfer).
Example: V = 12 V, R = 2 Ω, k = 0.02 N m/A. No-load speed 600 rad/s (about 5730 rpm), stall torque 0.12 N m, stall current 6 A, maximum output power 18 W.

Operating diagram
Draw the motor's torque–speed line and the load's torque–speed curve on the same axes; the steady operating point is where they cross (motor torque = load torque).
For a constant load torque of 0.03 N m in the example:
- I = T/k = 1.5 A; ω = (12 − 1.5 × 2)/0.02 = 450 rad/s.
- Output power = 0.03 × 450 = 13.5 W; input power = 12 × 1.5 = 18 W; efficiency 75%. The 4.5 W difference is the I²R loss in the armature (friction neglected).
Raising V shifts the line upward in parallel, which is how speed is controlled (often by PWM).

Gearboxes
A gearbox with ratio n (motor turns n times per output turn) multiplies torque by n and divides speed by n (ideal). The load torque reflected to the motor is T_load/n; the inertia reflected is J_load/n². Choosing n so that the reflected load sits near the motor's best region (for example near maximum power or maximum efficiency) is a key design decision.

Other actuators
- Solenoid: a coil pulls an iron plunger to reduce the reluctance of the magnetic path; short stroke, used for valves and locks.
- Stepper motor: moves in fixed steps (e.g. 1.8° per step, 200 steps per revolution) when its coils are energised in sequence; open-loop positioning, but can lose steps if overloaded.
- Brushless DC motors use electronic commutation; servo motors combine a motor with position feedback.
- Relays use a solenoid to operate switch contacts.

Exam tips: always start from V = IR + kω and T = kI; sketch the operating diagram with both characteristics labelled; and check units (rad/s, not rpm, in the equations).

notes.h: Electromagnetic induction, magnetic circuits and transformers
notes.body:
Faraday's and Lenz's laws
- A changing magnetic flux linkage induces an emf: e = −N dΦ/dt (Faraday). The minus sign expresses Lenz's law: the induced current opposes the change that caused it.
- A conductor of length L moving at speed v across a field B has emf e = BLv. This is the generator principle and the source of back emf in motors.

Inductance
- Self-inductance L = NΦ/I (flux linkage per amp), so v = L di/dt.
- Mutual inductance couples two coils sharing flux; it is the basis of transformers and LVDTs.

Magnetic circuits
Magnetic circuits are analysed like electric circuits:
- Magnetomotive force (mmf) F = NI (ampere-turns) ↔ voltage.
- Flux Φ (Wb) ↔ current.
- Reluctance S = l/(μ₀μ_r A) ↔ resistance, with μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m.
- Φ = NI/S, and the inductance of a coil is L = N²/S.
Example: an iron core with path length 0.2 m, area 4 × 10⁻⁴ m², μ_r = 2000, wound with 500 turns:
- S_iron = 0.2/(4π × 10⁻⁷ × 2000 × 4 × 10⁻⁴) ≈ 1.99 × 10⁵ A/Wb, so L = 500²/1.99 × 10⁵ ≈ 1.26 H.
- Adding a 1 mm air gap (μ_r = 1) adds S_gap = 0.001/(4π × 10⁻⁷ × 4 × 10⁻⁴) ≈ 1.99 × 10⁶ A/Wb, ten times the iron's reluctance; L falls to about 0.114 H.
Even a small air gap dominates the reluctance. (Real iron saturates at high flux density, typically somewhere around 1.5–2 T for electrical steels, approximate, so these linear results hold only below saturation.)

The ideal transformer
Two coils (N₁ primary, N₂ secondary turns) on a common core. An alternating primary current produces an alternating flux that links both coils.
- Voltage ratio: V₁/V₂ = N₁/N₂.
- Current ratio (power conserved in an ideal transformer): I₁/I₂ = N₂/N₁.
- Impedance seen at the primary: Z₁ = (N₁/N₂)² Z₂.
Example: a 230 V to 12 V transformer has N₁/N₂ = 19.2. A 6 Ω load draws 2 A from the secondary; the primary current is 2 × 12/230 = 0.104 A, and the load appears at the primary as about 2200 Ω.
Transformers work only with alternating current: a steady DC current gives a constant flux and therefore no induced emf.

Real transformer losses
- Copper losses: I²R in the windings.
- Iron (core) losses: hysteresis (repeated magnetising of the core) and eddy currents (induced circulating currents in the core). Eddy currents are reduced by building the core from thin insulated laminations or using ferrite.
- Leakage flux and magnetising current; large transformers are still very efficient (often well above 95%, approximate).

Mechatronics applications
Isolation and step-down transformers in power supplies, current transformers for measurement, LVDT position sensors, inductive proximity sensors, and induction in motor windings and generators. A gearbox is the mechanical analogue of a transformer: speed (voltage) and torque (current) are traded by the ratio, and inertia (impedance) is reflected by the ratio squared.

Exam tips: keep turns ratio and impedance ratio distinct (impedance scales with the square), and in magnetic circuits add reluctances in series exactly as you would resistors.

cards.b: i = C dv/dt; energy ½Cv². Voltage cannot change instantaneously; open circuit at DC steady state.
v = L di/dt; energy ½Li². Current cannot change instantaneously; short circuit at DC steady state.
R = R₁R₂/(R₁ + R₂); always less than the smaller resistor.
v_out = v_in R₂/(R₁ + R₂), where R₂ is the resistor the output is taken across.
Mass corresponds to inductance (F = m dv/dt ↔ v = L di/dt).
Damper ↔ resistor (F = cv ↔ v = Ri); spring stiffness k ↔ 1/C.
With current entering the + terminal, p = vi is the power absorbed by the element; negative p means it delivers power.
V_rms = V_p/√2 ≈ 0.707V_p. UK mains: 230 V rms, about 325 V peak, 50 Hz.
The DC value that would dissipate the same average power in a resistor: √(mean of v²).
For 0/V switching with duty cycle D: mean = DV, RMS = V√D.
V_ref/2ⁿ for an n-bit converter; e.g. 5 V over 10 bits ≈ 4.9 mV per step.
Sample at more than twice the highest signal frequency (f_s > 2f_max) to avoid aliasing.
A frequency above f_s/2 appears after sampling as a false lower frequency; prevented by an anti-aliasing low-pass filter.

cards.f: Mean of a full-wave rectified sine
cards.b: 2V_p/π ≈ 0.637V_p (half-wave: V_p/π).
NOT(A·B) = Ā + B̄ and NOT(A + B) = Ā·B̄.
A gate type (NAND or NOR) from which any logic function can be built.
Output 1 when the inputs differ: A ⊕ B = ĀB + AB̄.
A + AB = A and A(A + B) = A.
OR of AND terms, one for each truth-table row whose output is 1.
Group adjacent 1s in blocks of 1, 2, 4 or 8 (wrapping round edges); each doubling removes one variable from the term.
Combinational: output depends only on current inputs. Sequential: also on stored state (latches, flip-flops).

cards.f: Range of an n-bit unsigned number
cards.b: 0 to 2ⁿ − 1, e.g. 0–255 for 8 bits.
GF = (ΔR/R)/ε; about 2 for metal-foil gauges (approximate).
v_out ≈ V_s × GF × ε/4 for one active gauge in a balanced Wheatstone bridge.
It nulls the large base resistance so a tiny change (e.g. 0.1 Ω in 120 Ω) gives a measurable voltage, and can cancel temperature effects.
360°/N for N lines per revolution; quadrature (×4) decoding improves this to 360°/(4N) and gives direction.
A junction of two dissimilar metals produces a voltage that depends on temperature difference: the basis of thermocouples.
Platinum resistance thermometer: 100 Ω at 0 °C, roughly 0.385 Ω/°C (approximate).
Different output for the same input depending on whether the input is increasing or decreasing.
Accuracy: closeness to the true value. Precision (repeatability): closeness of repeated readings to each other.
The algebraic sum of currents at a node is zero (charge is conserved).
The algebraic sum of voltages around any closed loop is zero (energy is conserved).
V_Th (open-circuit voltage) in series with R_Th (resistance seen with sources turned off).
When R_L = R_Th; P_max = V_Th²/(4R_Th) and efficiency is 50%.
RC circuit: τ = RC. RL circuit: τ = L/R. 63.2% of the change after τ, over 99% after 5τ.
The intersection of the source characteristic and the load characteristic on a v–i (or torque–speed) graph.
Replace ideal voltage sources by short circuits and ideal current sources by open circuits.
About 0.6–0.7 V when conducting; the constant-voltage-drop model uses 0.7 V.
About V_p − 1.4 V, because two diodes conduct in series in each half-cycle.

cards.f: Ripple frequency of a full-wave rectifier
cards.b: Twice the supply frequency (100 Hz from 50 Hz mains); half-wave gives the supply frequency.

cards.f: Approximate ripple with a reservoir capacitor
cards.b: ΔV ≈ I/(f_r C), with f_r the ripple frequency.
A diode designed to operate in reverse breakdown, holding a nearly constant voltage; used with a series resistor as a simple regulator.
A diode in reverse across an inductive load that gives the inductor current a path when switched off, preventing a damaging voltage spike.
Z_L = jωL; current lags voltage by 90°.
Z_C = 1/(jωC) = −j/(ωC); current leads voltage by 90°.

cards.f: Real power in an AC circuit
cards.b: P = V_rms I_rms cos φ, where cos φ is the power factor; dissipated only in resistance.
S = V_rms I_rms (VA); Q = V_rms I_rms sin φ (var); S² = P² + Q².
f_c = 1/(2πRC): the −3 dB point; e.g. 1 kΩ and 1 μF give about 159 Hz.
ω₀ = 1/√(LC): X_L = X_C, impedance purely resistive and minimum.

cards.f: Mechanical impedance of a mass, damper and spring
cards.b: F/v: mass jωm, damper c, spring k/(jω).
T = kI: torque is proportional to armature current.
V = IR + kω (steady state), where kω is the back emf.
ω₀ = V/k; T_s = kV/R (stall current V/R).

cards.f: Maximum mechanical power of a DC motor
cards.b: At half stall torque and half no-load speed: P_max = V²/(4R).
The intersection of the motor's torque–speed line with the load's torque–speed curve.

cards.f: Effect of a gearbox (ratio n, ideal)
cards.b: Output torque × n, output speed ÷ n; load torque reflected to motor ÷ n, inertia ÷ n².
F = BIL for a conductor perpendicular to the field.
Rotates in fixed angular steps (e.g. 1.8°) as coils are energised in sequence; open-loop positioning.
e = −N dΦ/dt: induced emf equals the rate of change of flux linkage; the minus sign is Lenz's law.
S = l/(μ₀μ_r A) in A/Wb; magnetic analogue of resistance, with Φ = NI/S.
L = N²/S; an air gap raises S sharply and lowers L.
V₁/V₂ = N₁/N₂ and I₁/I₂ = N₂/N₁ (power conserved).
A load Z₂ on the secondary appears at the primary as (N₁/N₂)²Z₂.
Only a changing flux induces an emf; DC gives a constant flux and no secondary voltage.
Thin insulated sheets break up the paths of eddy currents induced in the core, reducing eddy-current loss.
A gearbox: it trades speed for torque by the ratio and reflects inertia by the ratio squared.

questions.q: A 10 Ω resistor is connected in parallel with a 15 Ω resistor, and the pair is in series with a 4 Ω resistor across a 12 V supply. What current flows from the supply?
questions.why: 10 ∥ 15 = 150/25 = 6 Ω; plus 4 Ω gives 10 Ω, so I = 12/10 = 1.2 A. 0.41 A comes from adding all three in series (29 Ω). 0.86 A is 12/14, from treating the parallel pair as if it were just its smaller resistor (10 Ω) and adding 4 Ω. 3.0 A uses only the 4 Ω resistor, ignoring the parallel pair.

questions.q: In the force–voltage analogy between mechanical and electrical systems, which electrical element corresponds to a mass?
questions.why: F = m dv/dt has the same form as v = L di/dt when force maps to voltage and velocity to current, so mass ↔ inductance. The capacitor corresponds to mass only in the other (force–current) analogy; in the force–voltage analogy it corresponds to a spring (1/C = k). A resistor corresponds to a damper. A voltage source corresponds to an applied force, not to a mass.

questions.q: Explain why a capacitor behaves as an open circuit and an inductor as a short circuit in a DC circuit at steady state, and state what quantity in each cannot change instantaneously.
markScheme: At steady state all voltages and currents are constant, so dv/dt = 0 and di/dt = 0
Capacitor: i = C dv/dt = 0, so no current: open circuit
Inductor: v = L di/dt = 0, so no voltage across it: short circuit
Capacitor voltage and inductor current are continuous (an instantaneous change would need infinite current or voltage)
questions.modelAnswer: In a DC circuit at steady state nothing is changing, so all time derivatives are zero. A capacitor obeys i = C dv/dt, so its current is zero: it acts as an open circuit, although it may hold a voltage. An inductor obeys v = L di/dt, so the voltage across it is zero: it acts as a short circuit (apart from its winding resistance), although it may carry a current. A capacitor's voltage cannot jump, since that would require infinite current; an inductor's current cannot jump, since that would require infinite voltage. These continuity conditions give the initial values in transient problems.

questions.q: A motor driver switches a 12 V supply on and off with a PWM duty cycle of 25%. What is the mean voltage applied?
questions.why: Mean = D × V = 0.25 × 12 = 3 V. 6 V is the RMS value V√D = 12 × 0.5. 9 V is (1 − D)V, the mean if the 25% were the off-time. 8.5 V is 12/√2, the RMS relationship for a sine wave, which does not apply to a PWM waveform.

questions.q: A vibration signal containing frequencies up to 400 Hz is to be digitised. What is the minimum sampling rate that satisfies the Nyquist criterion?
questions.why: The sampling rate must exceed twice the highest frequency: f_s > 2 × 400 = 800 Hz (in practice a margin is added). 400 Hz equals the maximum frequency itself, so the 400 Hz component would alias. 200 Hz halves rather than doubles the frequency. 2513 Hz is 2π × 400, i.e. converting to an angular frequency in rad/s, which is not what the criterion uses.

questions.q: A 10-bit ADC with a 0–5 V input range digitises a temperature sensor whose output is 10 mV/°C. What is the voltage resolution, and what temperature change does one step represent? Suggest one way to improve the temperature resolution.
markScheme: Resolution = 5/2¹⁰ = 5/1024 ≈ 4.9 mV
Temperature step = 4.9/10 ≈ 0.49 °C
Improvement: amplify the sensor signal to use the full ADC range
or use a higher-resolution ADC (e.g. 12-bit gives ≈ 1.2 mV, ≈ 0.12 °C) or a smaller reference voltage
questions.modelAnswer: A 10-bit converter has 2¹⁰ = 1024 levels, so each step is 5/1024 = 4.88 mV. At 10 mV/°C, one step corresponds to 0.488 °C, so the reading is resolved only to about half a degree. The resolution could be improved by amplifying the sensor signal so its expected range fills the 0–5 V input, by reducing the ADC reference voltage to match the signal range, or by using a 12-bit converter, which gives 5/4096 = 1.22 mV, or about 0.12 °C per step.

questions.q: Which expression is equivalent to NOT(A AND B)?
questions.why: De Morgan: the complement of a product is the sum of the complements, so NOT(A·B) = Ā + B̄. Ā·B̄ is NOT(A + B), the NOR function: it comes from complementing the variables but forgetting to change AND to OR. A + B drops the complement altogether. Ā·B + A·B̄ is XOR, which is 0 when both inputs are 0, whereas NAND is 1 then.

questions.q: Simplify the Boolean expression Y = AB + AB̄ + ĀB.
questions.why: AB + AB̄ = A, so Y = A + ĀB = (A + Ā)(A + B) = A + B. Stopping after the first step and dropping ĀB gives just A. AB is the first term alone. A ⊕ B = AB̄ + ĀB omits the AB term, so it is 0 when both inputs are 1, unlike Y.

questions.q: A conveyor motor M must run when the start button S is on and the emergency stop E is not pressed (E = 1 when pressed), unless the overload sensor O = 1. Write a truth table, a Boolean expression for M, and implement it using only NAND gates.
markScheme: Truth table for S, E, O with M = 1 only for S = 1, E = 0, O = 0
M = S·Ē·Ō
Recognises M = NOT(NAND(S, Ē, Ō)) or uses De Morgan
NAND-only: inverters for E and O made from NAND gates with tied inputs, a three-input NAND, then a NAND inverter
Gate count/diagram clearly described
questions.modelAnswer: Of the eight input combinations, only S = 1, E = 0, O = 0 gives M = 1; all other rows give M = 0. Hence M = S·Ē·Ō. To use only NAND gates: make Ē and Ō with two NAND gates whose inputs are tied together (a NAND with both inputs equal to X gives X̄). Feed S, Ē and Ō into a three-input NAND, giving NOT(S·Ē·Ō). Finally invert that with another tied-input NAND to obtain M = S·Ē·Ō. That is four NAND gates in total. (In a real machine the emergency stop would also break the power circuit directly, not rely only on logic.)

questions.q: A 120 Ω strain gauge with gauge factor 2.0 is bonded to a component that experiences 500 microstrain. What is the change in resistance?
questions.why: ΔR = GF × ε × R = 2.0 × 500 × 10⁻⁶ × 120 = 0.12 Ω. 0.06 Ω omits the gauge factor (ε × R only). 120 Ω takes 500 microstrain as 0.5 (dropping the micro prefix): 2.0 × 0.5 × 120 = 120 Ω, an impossibly large change. 0.24 Ω applies the gauge factor twice.

questions.q: An incremental optical encoder with 500 lines per revolution is read with quadrature (×4) decoding. What is its angular resolution?
questions.why: ×4 decoding gives 4 × 500 = 2000 counts per revolution, so 360°/2000 = 0.18°. 0.72° is 360°/500, ignoring the quadrature decoding. 2.88° multiplies 0.72° by 4 instead of dividing. 0.09° assumes 4000 counts, i.e. ×8 decoding, which a two-channel quadrature encoder does not provide.

questions.q: A single 120 Ω strain gauge (GF = 2.0) forms one arm of a Wheatstone bridge whose other arms are fixed 120 Ω resistors, supplied at 5 V. Estimate the bridge output at a strain of 500 με, explain why the bridge is used, and suggest how temperature effects could be reduced.
markScheme: Balanced at zero strain (all arms equal), so output zero
Bridge measures the small change relative to a balanced reference; output then amplified
Temperature compensation: dummy gauge in adjacent arm (unstrained, same temperature) or half/full bridge
questions.modelAnswer: With all four arms at 120 Ω the bridge is balanced and gives zero output. Under 500 με, ΔR = 2 × 500 × 10⁻⁶ × 120 = 0.12 Ω. For a small change, a quarter bridge gives v_out ≈ V_s(ΔR/R)/4 = V_s GF ε/4 = 5 × 2 × 5 × 10⁻⁴/4 = 1.25 mV (an exact calculation gives 1.249 mV). Measuring 0.12 Ω directly against 120 Ω would need extremely precise resistance measurement; the bridge removes the large base value so only the change appears, and the millivolt output can then be amplified. Temperature changes the gauge resistance and expands the component; placing an identical unstrained 'dummy' gauge at the same temperature in an adjacent arm cancels this, and a half or full bridge with gauges in tension and compression both cancels temperature and increases sensitivity.

questions.q: A 12 V source feeds a voltage divider of 6 kΩ (top) and 3 kΩ (bottom), with the output taken across the 3 kΩ resistor. What is the Thévenin equivalent at the output?
questions.why: Open-circuit voltage = 12 × 3/(6 + 3) = 4 V. With the source shorted, the two resistors are in parallel: 6 × 3/9 = 2 kΩ. 9 kΩ adds them in series, forgetting that shorting the source puts them in parallel. 8 V is the voltage across the 6 kΩ resistor, the wrong arm of the divider. 12 V with 3 kΩ ignores the divider altogether.

questions.q: A 100 μF capacitor charges from 0 V through a 10 kΩ resistor from a 12 V supply. What is its voltage after 2 s?
questions.why: τ = RC = 10 000 × 100 × 10⁻⁶ = 1 s, so v = 12(1 − e⁻²) = 12 × 0.865 = 10.4 V. 7.6 V is 12(1 − e⁻¹), the value after one time constant (1 s), not two. 1.6 V is 12e⁻², the remaining difference from the final value, i.e. the discharging formula. 12 V assumes charging is complete, which takes about 5τ.

questions.q: For the 6 kΩ/3 kΩ divider on a 12 V supply, find the load resistance that receives maximum power, that power, and the efficiency of power delivery at that condition. Explain why electronic power supplies are not designed for maximum power transfer.
markScheme: V_Th = 4 V, R_Th = 2 kΩ
Maximum power when R_L = R_Th = 2 kΩ
P_max = V_Th²/(4R_Th) = 2 mW
Efficiency of the Thévenin model 50% (half the power lost in R_Th)
Power systems aim for high efficiency, so they use R_L ≫ R_source; maximum power transfer matters for signals
questions.modelAnswer: The Thévenin equivalent is 4 V with R_Th = 2 kΩ. Maximum power is transferred when R_L = R_Th = 2 kΩ: the load voltage is then 2 V and P = 2²/2000 = 2 mW (equivalently V_Th²/4R_Th = 16/8000). The same current flows through R_Th, so an equal 2 mW is dissipated inside the equivalent source: the efficiency is 50%. (In the actual divider the internal losses differ, but the load sees the same behaviour.) For power delivery, wasting half the energy is unacceptable, so supplies are designed with very low source resistance compared with the load (R_L ≫ R_source) to get high efficiency and good voltage regulation. Maximum power transfer matters mainly where the signal is weak, such as sensors, antennas and audio.

questions.q: A transformer gives 12 V rms to a bridge rectifier made of silicon diodes (0.7 V each). Approximately what is the peak DC output voltage?
questions.why: The peak is 12√2 = 16.97 V, and two diodes conduct in series in a bridge, so 16.97 − 1.4 = 15.6 V. 16.3 V subtracts only one diode drop (a half-wave or centre-tapped circuit). 10.6 V subtracts the two drops from the RMS value instead of the peak. 17.0 V ignores the diode drops completely.

questions.q: A full-wave rectifier on 50 Hz mains supplies 0.5 A to a load through a 2200 μF reservoir capacitor. What is the approximate peak-to-peak ripple?
questions.why: ΔV ≈ I/(f_r C) with f_r = 100 Hz for full-wave: 0.5/(100 × 2.2 × 10⁻³) = 2.3 V. 4.5 V uses 50 Hz, the half-wave ripple frequency. 1.1 V is half the correct figure: it confuses the peak-to-peak ripple with the ripple amplitude (half of peak-to-peak). 0.23 V comes from taking the capacitance as 22 mF, a factor-of-ten slip when converting 2200 μF.

questions.q: A microcontroller switches a 12 V relay coil through a transistor. Explain why a diode is connected across the coil, and which way round it goes.
markScheme: Coil is an inductor: v = L di/dt
When the transistor turns off, the current cannot stop instantly, so a large voltage spike appears
Spike can exceed the transistor's breakdown voltage and destroy it
Diode is reverse-biased in normal operation (cathode to +12 V) and conducts only to circulate the decaying coil current
questions.modelAnswer: A relay coil is an inductor, so v = L di/dt, and its current cannot change instantaneously. When the transistor switches off, the circuit tries to stop the current almost instantly, so di/dt is huge and a large voltage spike (often hundreds of volts) appears across the transistor, which can break it down. A flyback diode is connected across the coil with its cathode to the +12 V side, so it is reverse-biased and passes no current while the relay is energised. At switch-off the coil voltage reverses, the diode conducts, and the coil current circulates through it and decays harmlessly, its stored energy ½Li² being dissipated in the coil resistance and diode. The voltage at the transistor is then limited to about 12.7 V.

questions.q: A 100 Ω resistor in series with a 0.5 H inductor is connected to 230 V rms at 50 Hz. What current flows?
questions.why: X_L = 2π × 50 × 0.5 = 157.1 Ω, |Z| = √(100² + 157.1²) = 186.2 Ω, so I = 230/186.2 = 1.24 A. 2.30 A ignores the inductor (230/100). 0.89 A adds the resistance and reactance arithmetically (257.1 Ω) instead of as perpendicular phasors. 1.46 A uses only the reactance (230/157.1), ignoring the resistor.

questions.q: An RC low-pass filter uses R = 1 kΩ and C = 1 μF. What is its cut-off frequency?
questions.why: f_c = 1/(2πRC) = 1/(2π × 10⁻³) = 159 Hz. 1000 Hz is 1/(RC), which is the cut-off as an angular frequency in rad/s, quoted wrongly as hertz. 6.28 kHz multiplies 1/(RC) by 2π instead of dividing. 1.59 kHz comes from a factor-of-ten slip, taking C as 0.1 μF.

questions.q: For the 100 Ω + 0.5 H series load on 230 V rms, 50 Hz, find the power factor, the real power, and the capacitance that, connected in parallel with the load, would raise the power factor to 1.
markScheme: φ = arctan(157.1/100) = 57.5°, pf = cos φ = 0.537 lagging
Reactive power of load Q = I²X_L = 239.7 var
Capacitor must supply Q: V²ωC = Q, so C = Q/(ωV²) ≈ 14.4 μF
Explains that the supply current then falls to P/V ≈ 0.66 A
questions.modelAnswer: Z = 100 + j157.1 Ω, so φ = arctan(1.571) = 57.5° and the power factor is cos 57.5° = 0.537 lagging. I = 230/186.2 = 1.235 A, so P = I²R = 1.235² × 100 = 152.6 W. The load's reactive power is Q = I²X_L = 1.525 × 157.1 = 239.7 var. A parallel capacitor draws reactive power V²ωC, of opposite sign, so for unity power factor V²ωC = Q, giving C = 239.7/(314.2 × 230²) = 239.7/1.662 × 10⁷ = 1.44 × 10⁻⁵ F ≈ 14.4 μF. The load itself is unchanged, but the supply now provides only the real power: I_supply = 152.6/230 = 0.66 A instead of 1.24 A, reducing cable losses.

questions.q: A permanent-magnet DC motor has k = 0.02 N m/A and armature resistance 2 Ω and runs from 12 V. What is its stall torque?
questions.why: At stall ω = 0 so there is no back emf: I = V/R = 6 A and T = kI = 0.02 × 6 = 0.12 N m. 0.24 N m multiplies k by V directly (0.02 × 12), forgetting to divide by the resistance. 600 N m is V/k, which is actually the no-load speed in rad/s, not a torque. 0.48 N m multiplies k by V × R instead of V/R.

questions.q: The same motor (12 V, 2 Ω, k = 0.02 N m/A) drives a constant load torque of 0.03 N m. What is its steady speed?
questions.why: I = T/k = 1.5 A, so the back emf is 12 − 1.5 × 2 = 9 V and ω = 9/0.02 = 450 rad/s. 600 rad/s is the no-load speed, ignoring the load. 150 rad/s is the speed drop (IR/k) rather than the speed itself. 300 rad/s is half the no-load speed, which assumes the motor runs at its maximum-power point; that applies only when the load torque is half the stall torque (0.06 N m), not 0.03 N m.

questions.q: Sketch the torque–speed and power–speed characteristics of a permanent-magnet DC motor and show that its maximum mechanical output power is V²/(4R).
markScheme: Torque–speed straight line from stall torque kV/R at ω = 0 to no-load speed V/k at T = 0
P = Tω with T = (k/R)(V − kω)
dP/dω = 0 gives ω = V/(2k), half no-load speed
At that speed T = kV/(2R), half stall torque
P_max = (V/2k)(kV/2R) = V²/(4R); power curve is a parabola, zero at stall and no load
questions.modelAnswer: From V = IR + kω and T = kI, T = (k/R)(V − kω): a straight line falling from the stall torque kV/R at ω = 0 to zero at the no-load speed V/k. Output power P = Tω = (k/R)(Vω − kω²), a parabola that is zero both at stall (no speed) and at no load (no torque). Setting dP/dω = (k/R)(V − 2kω) = 0 gives ω = V/(2k), half the no-load speed; the torque there is (k/R)(V − V/2) = kV/(2R), half the stall torque. Hence P_max = [V/(2k)][kV/(2R)] = V²/(4R). At this point half the input power is lost in R (efficiency 50%), so motors are usually run at lower torque and higher speed for efficiency, with maximum power used only for short bursts.

questions.q: An ideal transformer steps 230 V down to 12 V and supplies a 6 Ω resistive load. What current flows in the primary?
questions.why: Secondary current = 12/6 = 2 A. Power is conserved, so I₁ = I₂ × N₂/N₁ = 2 × 12/230 = 0.104 A. 2.0 A is the secondary current. 38.3 A multiplies by the turns ratio instead of dividing (2 × 230/12). 0.0054 A divides by the ratio twice, as if applying the impedance (squared) ratio to current.

questions.q: A 500-turn coil on an iron core (reluctance 2.0 × 10⁵ A/Wb) has a 1 mm air gap cut into the core, adding 2.0 × 10⁶ A/Wb. Approximately what is the new inductance?
questions.why: Reluctances in series add: 2.0 × 10⁵ + 2.0 × 10⁶ = 2.2 × 10⁶ A/Wb, so L = N²/S = 250 000/2.2 × 10⁶ = 0.11 H. 1.25 H is the inductance without the gap. 0.125 H uses the gap reluctance alone, ignoring the iron. 1.38 H combines the reluctances as if they were in parallel (giving 1.8 × 10⁵ A/Wb), which wrongly increases L; the flux must pass through the iron and the gap in turn, so they are in series.

questions.q: Explain, using Faraday's law, how a transformer changes voltage, and why real transformer cores are laminated.
markScheme: AC in primary produces alternating flux in the core, linking both coils
Faraday: e = N dΦ/dt in each coil, same dΦ/dt, so V₁/V₂ = N₁/N₂
Changing flux also induces eddy currents in a conducting core, causing I²R heating
Thin insulated laminations restrict eddy current paths and reduce the loss
questions.modelAnswer: An alternating current in the primary sets up an alternating flux in the iron core, which guides nearly all of it through the secondary as well. By Faraday's law each turn has emf dΦ/dt, so the primary and secondary emfs are N₁dΦ/dt and N₂dΦ/dt, and V₁/V₂ = N₁/N₂. The same changing flux also induces emfs inside the iron core itself, which is a conductor, so circulating eddy currents flow and heat it (I²R loss). Building the core from thin sheets insulated from one another breaks these current paths into narrow loops of higher resistance, greatly reducing eddy-current losses. Hysteresis losses are reduced separately by using soft magnetic steels.

questions.q:
A small winch uses a permanent-magnet DC motor (supply 24 V, armature resistance 1.5 Ω, k = 0.05 N m/A) driving a drum of radius 50 mm through an ideal gearbox of ratio 20:1 (motor turns 20 times per drum turn). It lifts a 10 kg mass at constant speed (g = 9.81 m/s²). Neglect friction and inertia.
(a) Find the motor's no-load speed and stall torque, and sketch its torque–speed characteristic. [5]
(b) Find the torque at the drum and at the motor, the motor current, motor speed and lifting speed. [8]
(c) Find the input power, output power and efficiency. [5]
(d) What is the largest mass the winch could just hold stationary? What gear ratio would give the maximum lifting power for the 10 kg load, and what lifting speed would that give? [7]
markScheme: (a) ω₀ = V/k = 480 rad/s; T_s = kV/R = 0.8 N m; straight line between them
(b) Drum torque = 10 × 9.81 × 0.05 = 4.905 N m; motor torque = 4.905/20 = 0.245 N m
(b) Drum speed 16.6 rad/s; lifting speed 0.83 m/s
(c) P_in = 24 × 4.905 = 117.7 W; P_out = mgv = 81.6 W; efficiency 69%
(d) At stall, drum torque = 0.8 × 20 = 16 N m, so m_max = 16/(9.81 × 0.05) = 32.6 kg
(d) Max power at half stall torque 0.4 N m, so n = 4.905/0.4 = 12.3; motor speed 240 rad/s
(d) Lifting speed = 240/12.26 × 0.05 = 0.98 m/s; output power V²/4R = 96 W
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) No-load speed ω₀ = V/k = 24/0.05 = 480 rad/s (about 4580 rpm). Stall current = 24/1.5 = 16 A, so stall torque T_s = kV/R = 0.05 × 16 = 0.8 N m. The torque–speed characteristic is a straight line from (ω = 0, T = 0.8 N m) to (ω = 480 rad/s, T = 0).

(b) The load force is mg = 98.1 N, so the drum torque is 98.1 × 0.05 = 4.905 N m. An ideal 20:1 gearbox divides this by 20, so the motor torque is 0.245 N m. Motor current I = T/k = 0.245/0.05 = 4.905 A. Back emf = 24 − 4.905 × 1.5 = 16.64 V, so ω = 16.64/0.05 = 332.9 rad/s. The drum turns at 332.9/20 = 16.64 rad/s, and the lifting speed is 16.64 × 0.05 = 0.832 m/s.

(c) Electrical input power = VI = 24 × 4.905 = 117.7 W. Mechanical output = mgv = 98.1 × 0.832 = 81.6 W (check: motor Tω = 0.245 × 332.9 = 81.6 W). Efficiency = 81.6/117.7 = 69%. The 36.1 W difference is armature copper loss I²R = 4.905² × 1.5.

(d) To hold a load stationary the motor works at stall: maximum drum torque = 0.8 × 20 = 16 N m, so the largest mass is 16/(9.81 × 0.05) = 32.6 kg (the motor would draw 16 A and overheat if held there for long). Maximum output power occurs at half stall torque (0.4 N m) and half no-load speed (240 rad/s), giving V²/(4R) = 576/6 = 96 W. For the 10 kg load to appear as 0.4 N m at the motor, n = 4.905/0.4 = 12.3. The drum would then turn at 240/12.26 = 19.6 rad/s, lifting at 0.98 m/s. The trade-off is efficiency: at maximum power the efficiency is only 50%, compared with 69% for the 20:1 gearbox, so a designer would usually prefer a ratio between these depending on whether speed or energy use matters more.

questions.q:
A DC supply for a mechatronic rig is built from a 230 V rms, 50 Hz mains transformer with a 12 V rms secondary, a bridge rectifier of silicon diodes (0.7 V each) and a reservoir capacitor. The load draws 0.5 A.
(a) Find the transformer turns ratio and the peak secondary voltage. [3]
(b) Find the peak DC output voltage and explain why two diode drops are subtracted. [4]
(c) Find the minimum reservoir capacitance for a peak-to-peak ripple of no more than 1 V, and the approximate mean output voltage. [6]
(d) What peak reverse voltage must each diode withstand? [2]
(e) The supply drives a relay coil and a 2 V LED indicator at 20 mA from a 5 V regulated rail. Explain what extra components are needed and calculate the LED resistor. [5]
markScheme: (b) Two diodes conduct in series each half-cycle, so V_out,peak = 16.97 − 1.4 = 15.6 V
(c) Ripple frequency 100 Hz; C ≥ I/(f_r ΔV) = 0.5/(100 × 1) = 5000 μF
(c) Mean ≈ peak − ΔV/2 ≈ 15.1 V
(d) Each diode must withstand about V_p ≈ 17 V reverse (in practice chosen with margin)
(e) Flyback diode across the relay coil (reverse-biased) to suppress inductive spike
(e) LED resistor R = (5 − 2)/0.02 = 150 Ω
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The turns ratio N₁/N₂ = V₁/V₂ = 230/12 = 19.2. The peak secondary voltage is 12√2 = 16.97 V.

(b) In each half-cycle current flows from the secondary through one diode, the load, and a second diode back to the transformer, so two forward drops of about 0.7 V are in series with the load. The peak DC output is therefore 16.97 − 1.4 = 15.6 V.

(c) A full-wave rectifier recharges the capacitor twice per mains cycle, so the ripple frequency is 100 Hz. Between peaks the capacitor supplies the load current, so ΔV ≈ I/(f_r C). For ΔV ≤ 1 V: C ≥ 0.5/(100 × 1) = 5 × 10⁻³ F = 5000 μF; a standard value at or above this would be chosen. The output then swings between about 15.6 V and 14.6 V, so its mean is roughly 15.6 − 0.5 = 15.1 V.

(d) When a pair of diodes is off, each blocking diode sees approximately the full peak voltage, about 17 V (V_p, minus one conducting diode drop). In practice a diode rated at several times this, such as 50 V or more, would be selected for margin against mains surges.

(e) A relay coil is inductive, so a flyback diode must be fitted across it, reverse-biased in normal operation (cathode to the positive supply), to carry the coil current when the driving transistor switches off and prevent a large L di/dt spike. The LED needs a series current-limiting resistor: R = (5 − 2)/0.02 = 150 Ω, dissipating 3 × 0.02 = 60 mW. The 5 V rail itself would come from a regulator fed by the 15 V smoothed supply.
